subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which of the following is a magnetic material?
questions.explain: Iron is a ferromagnetic material, whereas copper, aluminium and brass are non-magnetic.

questions.q: What happens when the north poles of two magnets are brought close together?
questions.explain: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

questions.q: Why is soft iron, rather than steel, used for the core of an electromagnet?
options: It is a permanent magnet that never loses magnetism
It is easily magnetised and easily demagnetised
It cannot be magnetised at all
It is a better electrical conductor than steel
questions.explain: Soft iron is magnetically soft, so it magnetises and demagnetises readily, ideal for a temporary electromagnet.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates charge Q, current I and time t?
questions.explain: Charge is the product of current and time, so Q = It (measured in coulombs).

questions.q: The potential difference across a component is best defined as the:
options: Electrical energy transferred per unit charge passing through it
Rate of flow of electrical energy
Opposition to the flow of current
questions.explain: P.d. is the work done (energy transferred) per unit charge, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).

questions.q: A charge of 60 C passes a point in a circuit in 20 s. What is the current?
questions.explain: Current I = Q / t = 60 / 20 = 3 A.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms, defined by R = V / I.

questions.q: Why is the current the same at every point in a simple series circuit?
options: Charge is used up as it flows round
Charge is conserved and there is only one path for it to flow
The voltage is the same everywhere
questions.explain: With a single loop and conserved charge, the same rate of charge flow (current) passes every point.

questions.q: Adding a second identical resistor in parallel with the first will cause the total resistance of that combination to:
questions.explain: Extra parallel paths give the current more routes, so the combined resistance falls below that of a single resistor.

questions.q: A component has a potential difference of 12 V across it and carries a current of 3 A. What is its resistance?
As its temperature rises, the resistance of a thermistor:
questions.explain: A thermistor's resistance decreases as temperature increases.

questions.q: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω are connected in series. What is their total resistance?
questions.explain: Series resistances add: R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.

questions.q: A metallic conductor at constant temperature obeys Ohm's law. This means that:
options: The current is directly proportional to the potential difference
The resistance increases as current increases
The current is inversely proportional to the potential difference
No current flows until a threshold voltage is reached
questions.explain: For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, I ∝ V, so resistance stays constant.

questions.q: In a correctly wired mains plug, the fuse is connected in the:
questions.explain: The fuse is placed in the live wire so that it disconnects the supply from the appliance when it melts.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of the earth wire connected to the metal case of an appliance?
options: To increase the current supplied to the appliance
To provide a low-resistance path so a large current blows the fuse if the case becomes live
To store excess charge on the case
To reduce the resistance of the live wire
questions.explain: If a fault makes the case live, the earth wire carries a large current that blows the fuse, disconnecting the supply.

questions.q: In UK mains wiring, which colour identifies the live wire?
questions.explain: The live wire is brown, the neutral is blue and the earth is green-and-yellow.

questions.q: Fleming's left-hand rule is used to find the direction of the:
options: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
Induced e.m.f. in a moving conductor
Magnetic field around a bar magnet
Current in a transformer secondary coil
questions.explain: Fleming's left-hand rule relates field, current and the resulting force (motor effect).

questions.q: A transformer has 1000 turns on the primary and 200 turns on the secondary. If 240 V is applied to the primary, what is the secondary voltage?
An e.m.f. is induced in a coil of wire when:
options: A steady direct current flows through it
The magnetic field passing through it changes
It is connected to a battery
questions.explain: Electromagnetic induction requires a changing magnetic field (or flux) linking the coil.

questions.q: A step-up transformer is one that:
options: Has more turns on the secondary coil than the primary coil
Has more turns on the primary coil than the secondary coil
Has equal turns on both coils
questions.explain: A step-up transformer increases voltage, which requires more turns on the secondary than the primary.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Physics (0625) syllabus; Electricity & Magnetism
